meta.descriptionEn: On 9 November 1979 a technician at NORAD loaded a test tape into the warning system, but never switched the system status to test. What followed was a stream of false warnings that spread to continuity-of-government bunkers and command posts around the world. Months later, in June 1980, a failed computer device did it again. Some commands put nuclear-armed planes into the air. Others stayed calm because their own radar and satellite reports showed nothing. How can one small human error and one faulty chip bring the world this close to the edge? What did commanders see, what did they decide, and what changed afterwards? This documentary uses only documented sources to tell the story of the false alarms inside Cheyenne Mountain.

articleEn: On 9 November 1979, a technician at NORAD loaded a test tape into a computer system. It looked like a small, routine job. But the technician did not switch the system's status to "test." That single omission set off a chain of false warnings around the world.

The false warnings reached two continuity of government bunkers, which exist to keep the government running in a crisis. They also spread to command posts around the world. Here was a danger being shown that did not exist. Imagine the system built to warn of an attack raising a false alarm itself.

This raises several questions. How did it happen? Could one person's mistake really cause so much trouble? Who trusted the data? How close did the danger actually come? And, most important, what changed afterward?

The story does not stop at one event. It starts with 1979, then looks at two more incidents in 1980. Finally it turns to 26 September 1983, when Soviet officer Stanislav Petrov faced a satellite warning and chose to wait. It is a story of a tape, a chip, and the question of how far we should trust machines.

articleEn: NORAD stands for North American Aerospace Defense Command. It is a bi-national mutual defense organization of Canada and the United States, known in French as CDAAN. Its headquarters is at Peterson Space Force Base in Colorado, which also hosts the headquarters of USNORTHCOM.

It was established on 12 September 1957 under the name North American Air Defense Command. The idea was put forward in late 1956 by the Joint Canadian–U.S. Military Group, and the US Joint Chiefs of Staff approved it in February 1957. It was announced in August 1957, and the command headquarters was set up on 12 September in the 1954 blockhouse at Ent Air Force Base.

In 1958 the two countries settled an important point: the NORAD commander would always be an American officer and the vice commander a Canadian. Canada accepted that the command's basic purpose would be early warning and defense of the retaliatory power of Strategic Air Command, or SAC. In simple terms, the first job was to see danger early, and the second was to keep safe the force that could answer it.

NORAD divides North America into three regions: the Alaskan Region, the Canadian Region and the American Continental Region. The Alaskan Regional Operations Control Center, or ROCC, is at Joint Base Elmendorf–Richardson, staffed by active duty personnel from the 11th Air Force and the Canadian Armed Forces. The Canadian Region headquarters is at CFB Winnipeg. In 1996 it was renamed 1 Canadian Air Division and moved from North Bay to Winnipeg.

The U.S. portion is the Continental NORAD Region, or CONR, which watches the airspace of the contiguous United States. CONR is the NORAD name for First Air Force, headquartered at Tyndall Air Force Base in Florida. The command structure runs from the commanding officer to the executive officer, the chief of staff and the commander senior enlisted leader. The Command Center at Peterson gathers information from sensors around the world so that leaders in Canada and the United States get an accurate picture of any threat.

By 1965 roughly 250,000 American and Canadian personnel were part of NORAD's operation, so it was no small system. Canada contributes CF-18 Hornet fighters, such as the squadrons at Cold Lake and Bagotville, as alert assets. In the United States, Air National Guard fighter wings with F-15 and F-16 aircraft handle the same air defense mission. The East and West sector control centers, at Rome, New York, and McChord Field, Washington, keep constant watch over the CONUS airspace. That was the shield two countries built together, and one of its key centers was hidden inside a mountain.

articleEn: Cheyenne Mountain Complex is a military installation built inside a mountain in El Paso County, Colorado. During the Cold War, hardened installations that could withstand Soviet attacks were considered essential. Tensions were already high: the Korean War, two Taiwan Strait crises, the 1961 Berlin Crisis and the Cuban Missile Crisis had all shown how near the nuclear threat was.

In August 1960 the bunker's mission was expanded. It was to become a center from which both space attack and air attack could be monitored. Excavation began on 18 May 1961. The United States Army Corps of Engineers was responsible for the work, and the Utah Construction & Mining Company did the drilling and blasting. Burroughs Corporation built the electronics and communications system, whose job was to evaluate aerospace surveillance data almost instantly.

Sources disagree on dates. One says Cheyenne Mountain Complex became operational on 6 February 1967. Another says NORAD began running the Combat Operations Center on 30 October 1964 and accepted the complex on 8 February 1966. The initial funds came to $142.4 million.

The complex was designed to remain partly protected against an attack by nuclear-tipped missiles. Its large network of tunnels lies beneath 2,000 feet of gravel, and sources say it can withstand a blast wave. Inside are fifteen three-story buildings resting on more than a thousand giant springs, so earthquakes or explosions do not shake them. The springs are designed to keep each building from shifting more than 1 inch, and the pipes have flexible connectors. Blast valves and special filters can block airborne chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear contaminants.

The complex has its own power plant, heating and cooling, and water supply. There is a 1.5 million gallon reservoir, and another of 4.5 million gallons serves as a heat sink. It also has a diesel fuel supply and a battery bank with redundant generators. Inside are a medical facility, a market, a cafeteria, fitness centers and suites for senior military officers. It was like a small city.

But none of this was for comfort. Several variants of the Soviet R-36 carried a single warhead of 18 to 25 megatons, and places like Cheyenne Mountain were targets. One secondhand account says a dozen or more warheads might be needed against such a target to make a first strike kill certain. One statement says the staff's job was to detect an incoming Soviet attack and help coordinate a quick response. It was a place where even wrong data could reach very big decisions, and in 1979 this very system began giving false warnings.

articleEn: This system did not appear overnight. It took years of work, money and machines. In late 1958 Canada and the United States began CADIN, Continental Air Defense Integration North, for the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment air defense network. In January 1959 the two countries signed a cost-sharing agreement. In December 1958 NORAD submitted two plans, with an average annual cost of about five and a half billion. That figure included the accelerated Nike Zeus program and three Ballistic Missile Early Warning System sites. Attention was no longer only on bomber aircraft.

NORAD's bunker at CFB North Bay in Canada was built between 1959 and 1963 and held the SAGE AN/FSQ-7 Combat Direction Central computer. Eight smaller U.S. Air Force AN/FSQ-8 systems also fed data to NORAD, and each could command the air defense of the whole United States. Older arrangements were ending: the RCAF's Long Range Air Raid Warning System closed, and the US Ground Observer Corps was deactivated in January 1959.

In August 1960 Cheyenne Mountain's mission was expanded to a hardened center from which actions against space and air attack could be run. In October 1960 the Secretary of Defense gave operational command of space surveillance to CONAD and operational control to NORAD. In December 1960 the JCS placed the Space Detection and Tracking System at Ent Air Force Base under CINCNORAD's operational control. In 1963 command center operations moved from Ent Air Force Base to the Chidlaw Building.

On 30 October 1964 NORAD began running Cheyenne Mountain's Combat Operations Center. In 1965 roughly 250,000 American and Canadian personnel were connected to NORAD's operation. On 8 February 1966 the Cheyenne Mountain Complex was formally accepted. From 15 November 1968 the Department of Defense began changes to the command organization, and by 1972 NORAD had eight regional areas for air defense.

Then came the 427M system, part of the Cheyenne Mountain Complex Improvements Program, which became operational in 1979. It had three major parts: CSS, NCS and SCC. The goal was to replace older systems with more reliable and faster early warning. But according to one account, the system was at first "wholly ineffective," and it caused several failures in the Worldwide Military Command and Control System. A system meant to build trust created problems at the start.

On 1 October 1979 the Space Defense Operations Center, SPADOC, was established. It brought satellite survivability, space surveillance and US ASAT operations together in a wartime hub. It used Honeywell H6080 computers, but by 1981 they could not meet computation needs on time.

The shape of the threat was also changing. The danger from crewed bomber aircraft was slowly giving way to intercontinental ballistic missiles. That is why Aerospace Defense Command was made inactive in 1980. The question was whether such large, complex machines could tell the truth every time.

articleEn: 9 November 1979 looks like an ordinary date, but inside NORAD a small mistake was about to travel far. A technician loaded a test tape into the system. One step remained: switching the system status to "test." That step was not taken, and the status did not go to test. The result was a stream of constant false warnings.

The warnings did not stay within NORAD. According to the source, they spread to two continuity of government bunkers and to command posts around the world. A continuity of government bunker is a place from which government can keep working in a crisis, so a false warning reaching it is no small matter. Air Force Gen. James V. Hartinger said his basic responsibility was to give Washington "timely, unambiguous, reliable warning." If clear warning is needed, a false warning is its direct opposite, which is what makes the event serious.

By 1978 the NORAD Combat Operations Center had five operating centers and a command post. A System Center gathered their information and showed it in the Command Post. The NORAD Computer System replaced the 425L Command and Control System, the Display Information Processor, the Command Center Processing System and other hardware. The aim was to centralize many databases, improve online displays, and combine the processing and transmission of warning information. The original UNIVAC 1106 of the Command Center Processing System was re-purposed as a backup, and the system was upgraded to a UNIVAC 1100/42.

Consider the timing. The 427M system became fully operational in 1979, and SPADOC was established on 1 October, about five and a half weeks before this event. Around then NORAD also built an off-site testing facility in Colorado Springs so system changes could be tested offline before going into production. The source places this in late 1979 or early 1980, so the exact date is unclear, but the purpose was plain: keep experiments separate from production.

Our sources do not say how long the warnings lasted or who first caught the error, so we will not guess. We only know that a test tape and an unchanged status switch were enough to send warnings to command posts around the world. About three weeks later, on 1 December 1979, SAC took control of ballistic missile warning and space surveillance facilities from ADCOM. The source ties this to the 1979 Joint US-Canada Air Defense Study, not to this event.

The incident was not alone. According to the source, NORAD systems failed on at least three occasions, and the other two came the next year, in June 1980. The lesson of 1979 is that a great danger can sometimes be not an enemy missile but a wrong setup of your own machine. But 1979 was only the beginning. Another fault was coming the next year, and this time different commands answered differently.

articleEn: Now to June 1980. On 3 June a computer communications device failed, and its effect reached U.S. Air Force command posts around the world. Warning messages began flashing intermittently at those posts, saying a nuclear attack was underway. Three days later, on 6 June 1980, the story repeated. Once again a failure of the computer communications device sent the same false messages.

Another source on the 1979 and 1980 events mentions a computer chip that "went haywire." One source speaks of a device and the other of a chip. They may be different words for the same fault, but the sources do not make this clear.

Now the most interesting part. According to the source, during these events Pacific Air Forces, PACAF, put its planes in the air with nuclear bombs aboard. The source uses the word "properly" for PACAF, meaning according to procedure. Strategic Air Command, SAC, did not do so. SAC was criticized for not following procedure. Yet according to the source, SAC knew these were almost certainly false alarms, and PACAF had the same sense. Both commands knew the warning was probably false, yet their responses were not the same.

How were both so sure? Both command posts had recently started receiving direct reports from radar, satellite and other detection systems. That information did not match the wrong data coming from NORAD, and the mismatch became the biggest clue. Imagine it: NORAD's data speaks of an attack while the reports from other detection systems do not agree. In this light the event was not only a machine fault. It was also a test of how different commands handle the same warning.

Note one thing: SAC was criticized for breaking procedure, not for failing to judge reality. Another source says Cheyenne Mountain staff analyzed the data and found the warnings were erroneous. Afterward, systems were updated so they could recognize false alarms. We will return to this in the next chapter.

Now to Gen. James V. Hartinger. He said that in 1979 and 1980 an average of about 6,700 messages per hour were generated, and that all were processed without error. That raises a question: where did the false warnings come from? Perhaps he meant ordinary message traffic, but that is only a guess, and the sources do not clarify the difference. According to one source, after another failure in 1980 the faulty computer chip was updated, and staff and commander processes were improved.

So where did the real difference come from in June 1980? According to the source, the direct reports from radar, satellite and other detection systems did not match NORAD's wrong data. But if different commands respond differently to the same warning, was the weakness only in hardware? In the next part we ask: who was to blame?

Staff analyzed the data and found the warnings erroneous. Why separate sources mattered, and how PACAF and SAC handled the same warning differently. Fixes: systems updated to identify false alarms, an off-site test facility, a replaced chip, improved commander and staff processes.

articleEn: So who was to blame? The sources do not put full responsibility on one person or one machine. Three aspects stand out. The first is human error. On 9 November 1979 a technician at NORAD loaded a test tape but did not switch the system status to "test." The system was not told this was only a test. As a result, continuous false warnings reached two continuity of government bunkers and command posts around the world.

The second is hardware. On 3 and 6 June 1980 a failure of a computer communications device made nuclear attack warnings flash in US Air Force command posts. Here the sources differ: one calls it a communications device failure, while another says a computer chip "went haywire."

The third is design and upgrades. Cheyenne Mountain's 427M system became fully operational in 1979, but according to one source it was "wholly ineffective" at first. The same source says this caused several failures in the Worldwide Military Command and Control System. The new system was itself troubled.

How was the false warning recognized as false? According to the source, staff analyzed the data and found the warnings were erroneous. The PACAF and SAC command posts had both recently started receiving direct radar and satellite reports, and these did not match NORAD's data. A warning was coming in, while independent sources did not confirm it.

Still, the two commands responded differently. According to the source, PACAF properly put in the air its planes loaded with nuclear bombs. SAC did not, and was criticized for not following procedure, even though SAC also felt almost sure these were false alarms.

Now the fixes. According to one source, systems were updated after these events so they could recognize false alarms. NORAD built an off-site testing facility in Colorado Springs so system changes could be tested offline before going into production. One source puts this in late 1979 or early 1980, while another mentions a Test and Development Facility at Peterson Air Force Base in 1982. After another 1980 failure, the faulty chip was updated, and staff and commander processes were improved to give a better response to warnings.

General James V. Hartinger of the Air Force said his basic responsibility was to give Washington "timely, unambiguous, reliable warning." He said that in 1979 and 1980 about 6,700 messages per hour were generated and all were processed without error. Here is a contradiction: on one side the claim that all messages were processed without error, on the other the false missile warnings in those same years.
So what is the real lesson? In our view, human error, hardware failure and design weakness can combine into a danger. Did everything truly change afterward? The next and final part looks at that.

articleEn: After the 1979 Joint US-Canada Air Defense Study, the command structure changed. On 1 December 1979 SAC took control of ballistic missile warning and space surveillance from ADCOM. Then on 31 March 1980 Aerospace Defense Command ceased to exist as a major command. ADCOM was formed from its Cheyenne Mountain organizations, and its commander was the same as NORAD's.

But upgrades were not easy. The November 1988 Cheyenne Mountain Upgrade was not installed because it was not compatible with other systems, and testing did not meet specifications. In 1986 Congress approved SCIS, but by 1992 it was delayed and the cost estimate had grown from 142 million to 234 million dollars. Granite Sentry was budgeted at 230 million dollars but slipped from 1993 to 1996. In 1997 testing, its nuclear detonation data processing proved inadequate. From February 1995 a 450 million dollar missile warning center upgrade began, part of Cheyenne Mountain's 1.7 billion dollar renovation program. In July 2006 the Cheyenne Mountain Realignment was announced to bring NORAD's daily operations together at Peterson, and in 2008 the complex became an alternate main operations center.

Now to 1983. On 26 September the Soviet system Oko reported the launch of one ICBM from the United States, followed by four more missiles. Stanislav Petrov was the duty officer at the Serpukhov-15 bunker. He doubted the warning and waited for confirmation that never came. It was later learned that the error came from a rare alignment of sunlight on high-altitude clouds and the satellites' Molniya orbits. Ground radar also gave no corroborating evidence.

Petrov found an attack of five missiles implausible because he had been told a US strike would be very large. But in a 2013 interview Petrov said he was not fully certain at the time that the alarm was false. His decision rested on judgment. According to Pavel Podvig, there were at least three decision-making layers above Petrov's command center, so the report would not go straight to a launch.

One thing is common to the stories of 1979, 1980 and 1983: relying on a single signal can be dangerous, and verification from separate sources is very important. Some questions remain open. In June 1980, was the fault in the chip or the communications device? The sources give no clear answer. What do you think? When machine and human opinion differ, which should we trust? shorts.text: صرف ایک tape نے دنیا بھر کے command posts میں خطرے کی گھنٹی بجا دی تھی۔ کیسے؟ تاریخ تھی 9 November 1979۔ NORAD میں ایک technician نے computer system میں ایک test tape load کی۔ کام چھوٹا سا تھا۔ لیکن ایک قدم رہ گیا۔ اس نے system کا status "test" پر switch نہیں کیا۔ بس یہی ایک غلطی کافی تھی۔ system سے مسلسل false warnings نکلنے لگیں۔ یہ warnings صرف NORAD تک نہیں رہیں۔ source کے مطابق یہ دو continuity of government bunkers تک پہنچیں، اور دنیا بھر کے command posts تک بھی۔ continuity of government bunker وہ جگہ ہوتی ہے جہاں سے بحران میں حکومت کا کام جاری رہ سکے۔ سوچیں، جو system حملے سے خبردار کرتا ہے، وہی غلط alarm بجا دے تو کیا ہوگا؟ اور کیا یہ آخری بار تھا؟ نہیں۔ کچھ ہی مہینوں بعد، June 1980 میں، کہانی دوبارہ دہرائی گئی۔ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Sirf aik tape ne dunya bhar ke command posts mein khatre ki ghanti baja di thi. Kaise? Tareekh thi 9 November 1979. NORAD mein aik technician ne computer system mein aik test tape load ki. Kaam chhota sa tha. Lekin aik qadam reh gaya. Us ne system ka status "test" par switch nahin kiya. Bas yehi aik ghalti kafi thi. System se musalsal false warnings nikalne lagin. Yeh warnings sirf NORAD tak nahin rahin. Source ke mutabiq yeh do continuity of government bunkers tak pahunchin, aur dunya bhar ke command posts tak bhi. continuity of government bunker woh jagah hoti hai jahan se bohran mein hukumat ka kaam jari reh sake. Sochein, jo system hamle se khabardar karta hai, wohi ghalat alarm baja de to kya hoga? Aur kya yeh aakhri baar tha? Nahin. Kuch hi mahino baad, June 1980 mein, kahani dobara dohrai gayi. Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 9 November 1979, a test tape loaded without switching the status to "test" triggered false warnings worldwide.
A short look at one small mistake inside NORAD.

shorts.titleEn: The Mountain Built to Resist Nuclear Attack
shorts.text: ایک پورے پہاڑ کے اندر bunker بنانے کا فیصلہ کیوں ہوا؟ جگہ تھی Cheyenne Mountain، Colorado۔ Cold War میں Soviet Union کے حملوں کے سامنے ٹک سکنے والی hardened installations ضروری سمجھی جاتی تھیں۔ August 1960 میں اس bunker کا mission بڑھا دیا گیا۔ اب یہاں سے space attack اور air attack، دونوں کی نگرانی ہونی تھی۔ پھر 18 May 1961 کو کھدائی شروع ہوئی۔ یہ کام United States Army Corps of Engineers کے ذمے تھا، اور drilling اور blasting Utah Construction & Mining Company نے کی۔ electronics اور communications system Burroughs Corporation نے بنانا تھا۔ ابتدائی funds 142.4 million dollars تھے۔ source کے مطابق کئی راستے 2,000 feet کی gravel کے نیچے blast wave سہہ سکتے ہیں۔ یہاں پندرہ تین منزلہ buildings ہیں، جو ایک ہزار سے زیادہ springs پر کھڑی ہیں۔ لیکن کیا یہ قلعہ واقعی کبھی آزمایا گیا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Aik poore pahaar ke andar bunker banane ka faisla kyun hua? Jagah thi Cheyenne Mountain, Colorado. Cold War mein Soviet Union ke hamlon ke samne tik sakne wali hardened installations zaroori samjhi jati thin. August 1960 mein is bunker ka mission barha diya gaya. Ab yahan se space attack aur air attack, dono ki nigrani honi thi. Phir 18 May 1961 ko khudai shuru hui. Yeh kaam United States Army Corps of Engineers ke zimme tha, aur drilling aur blasting Utah Construction & Mining Company ne ki. electronics aur communications system Burroughs Corporation ne banana tha. Ibtidai funds 142.4 million dollars thay. Source ke mutabiq kai raastay 2,000 feet ki gravel ke neeche blast wave saha sakte hain. Yahan pandrah teen manzila buildings hain, jo aik hazar se zyada springs par khari hain. Lekin kya yeh qila waqai kabhi aazmaya gaya? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Cheyenne Mountain Complex was dug into a Colorado mountain starting 18 May 1961, designed to be partially resistant to nuclear-tipped missile attack.
Here is how the bunker was planned and built.

shorts.titleEn: The Officer Who Doubted 5 Missiles in 1983
shorts.text: اگر امریکہ حملہ کرتا تو صرف پانچ missiles کیوں بھیجتا؟ یہی سوال 26 September 1983 کو Stanislav Petrov کے ذہن میں آیا۔ وہ Soviet Air Defence Forces کے lieutenant colonel تھے اور Oko early-warning system کے command center میں duty پر تھے۔ system نے بتایا کہ امریکہ سے ایک ICBM آ رہا ہے، اور پھر چار اور۔ Petrov کو شک ہوا۔ ان کے مطابق first strike بڑا ہوتا، اس لیے پانچ missiles بے معنی لگے۔ launch detection system نیا تھا، اور ground radar نے کوئی ثبوت نہیں دیا۔ وہ corroboration کا انتظار کرتے رہے، جو کبھی نہیں آئی۔ بعد میں پتا چلا کہ بادلوں پر سورج کی روشنی اور satellites کے Molniya orbits کی ایک نایاب alignment نے false alarm بنایا تھا۔ sources اس بارے میں مختلف ہیں کہ انہوں نے اپنے superiors کو بتایا یا نہیں۔ تو اس فیصلے کے بعد Petrov کے ساتھ کیا ہوا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Agar America hamla karta to sirf paanch missiles kyun bhejta? Yehi sawal 26 September 1983 ko Stanislav Petrov ke zehen mein aaya. Woh Soviet Air Defence Forces ke lieutenant colonel thay aur Oko early-warning system ke command center mein duty par thay. System ne bataya ke America se aik ICBM aa raha hai, aur phir chaar aur. Petrov ko shak hua. Un ke mutabiq first strike bara hota, is liye paanch missiles be-maani lage. launch detection system naya tha, aur ground radar ne koi saboot nahin diya. Woh corroboration ka intezar karte rahe, jo kabhi nahin aayi. Baad mein pata chala ke baadlon par sooraj ki roshni aur satellites ke Molniya orbits ki aik nayab alignment ne false alarm banaya tha. Sources is bare mein mukhtalif hain ke unhon ne apne superiors ko bataya ya nahin. To is faisle ke baad Petrov ke sath kya hua? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 26 September 1983 the Oko system reported five incoming missiles, and Stanislav Petrov doubted the warning.
A look at why he suspected a false alarm.
